section.title: The Linen Belt
section.sectionRationale: Jeremiah is sent on two strange errands, burying a fine linen loincloth until it rots, and watching wineskins smashed, both acted parables of Judah's ruined pride. The chapter ends with a piercing question: can a leopard change its spots? Judah's sin has become so ingrained that only God's own intervention, not self-effort, can address it.
section.thesis: Judah was meant to cling to the LORD as intimately as a loincloth clings to the waist, for His renown and praise and glory, but pride and habitual sin have ruined that closeness so completely that Judah is now as useless as a rotted garment, and as unable to change on its own as a leopard is to change its spots.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the linen loincloth buried and ruined, a sign act of Judah's spoiled closeness to God; the wineskins that will be smashed together, a picture of coming drunken judgment; the call to give glory to the LORD before darkness falls, extended even to the king and queen mother; and the piercing question, can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard its spots, exposing sin too ingrained for self-reform.

units.label: Buy yourself a linen loincloth
units.note: a sign act of ruined closeness to God

verses.text: This is what the LORD said to me: “Go and buy yourself a linen {{ezor|loincloth}} and put it around your waist, but do not let it touch water.”
So I bought a loincloth as the LORD had instructed me, and I put it around my waist.
Then the word of the LORD came to me a second time:
“Take the loincloth that you bought and are wearing, and go at once to Perath and hide it there in a crevice of the rocks.”
So I went and hid it at Perath, as the LORD had commanded me.
Many days later the LORD said to me, “Arise, go to Perath, and get the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there.”
So I went to Perath and dug up the loincloth, and I took it from the place where I had hidden it. But now it was ruined, of no use at all.
Then the word of the LORD came to me:
“This is what the LORD says: In the same way I will ruin the {{gaon|pride}} of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.

These evil people, who refuse to listen to My words, who follow the stubbornness of their own hearts, and who go after other gods to serve and worship them, they will be like this loincloth, of no use at all.

For just as a loincloth {{davaq|clings}} to a man’s waist, so I have made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to Me, declares the LORD, so that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory. But they did not listen.

Therefore you are to tell them that this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Every wineskin shall be filled with wine.’ 
And when they reply, ‘Don’t we surely know that every wineskin should be filled with wine?’

then you are to tell them that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am going to fill with drunkenness all who live in this land, the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the people of Jerusalem.
I will smash them against one another, fathers and sons alike, declares the LORD. I will allow no mercy or pity or compassion to keep Me from destroying them.’”

units.label: Give glory to the LORD before He brings darkness

verses.text: Listen and give heed. Do not be arrogant, for the LORD has spoken.
Give glory to the LORD your God before He brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the dusky mountains. You wait for light, but He turns it into deep gloom and thick darkness.
But if you do not listen, I will weep in secret because of your pride. My eyes will overflow with tears, because the LORD’s flock has been taken captive.
Say to the king and to the queen mother: “Take a lowly seat, for your glorious crowns have fallen from your heads.”
The cities of the Negev have been shut tight, and no one can open them. All Judah has been carried into exile, wholly taken captive.

units.label: Can the leopard change its spots?

verses.text: Lift up your eyes and see those coming from the north. Where is the flock entrusted to you, the sheep that were your pride?
What will you say when He sets over you close allies whom you yourself trained? Will not pangs of anguish grip you, as they do a woman in labor?

And if you ask yourself, “Why has this happened to me?” It is because of the magnitude of your iniquity that your skirts have been stripped off 
and your body has been exposed.
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his {{chabarburah|spots}}? Neither are you able to do good, you who are accustomed to doing evil.
“I will scatter you like chaff driven by the desert wind.
This is your lot, the portion I have measured to you,” declares the LORD, “because you have forgotten Me and trusted in falsehood.
So I will pull your skirts up over your face, that your shame may be seen.
Your adulteries and lustful neighings, your shameless prostitution on the hills and in the fields, I have seen your detestable acts. Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will you remain unclean?”

ezor.gloss: A loincloth or waistband, often a finely made garment worn close to the body. Its intimate closeness to the wearer becomes the sign act's central point, picturing how closely God intended Israel to cling to Him.

davaq.gloss: To cling, cleave, or stay closely attached. This is the same verb used of a husband clinging to his wife in Genesis 2:24, showing God intended a marriage-like closeness with His people, the very closeness pride and idolatry had ruined.

gaon.gloss: Pride, majesty, or exaltation, capable of positive or negative use depending on its object. Here it names the self-exalting pride God will ruin, exactly as the loincloth was ruined, since Judah's pride had displaced its intended closeness to God.

chabarburah.gloss: Spots or markings, used of a leopard's fixed, natural pattern. The rhetorical question exposes that Judah's habitual evil has become as fixed as an animal's markings, requiring God's own transforming work, not mere willpower, to change.

basic.context: God sends Jeremiah on two strange errands. First, he buys a fine linen loincloth, wears it, then buries it by Perath until it rots, useless, a picture of how Judah, meant to cling to the LORD as closely and beautifully as that garment clung to Jeremiah's waist, has ruined that closeness through pride. Second, wineskins will be smashed together in coming judgment. The chapter ends with Jeremiah's own tears and a devastating question: can a leopard change its spots? Judah's sin has become second nature, and only God can address what habit cannot undo.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic street theatre, an enacted parable meant to be seen and remembered, not merely heard, in a culture where visual sign acts carried as much authority as spoken oracles. The rhetorical question about the Ethiopian and the leopard is not a claim that people never change, but an exposure that such change cannot come from the self alone; it requires God's own transforming work.
basic.originalLanguages: The loincloth, ezor, was meant to davaq, cling, to a man's body exactly as Israel was meant to cling to the LORD, the same verb used of a husband clinging to his wife in Genesis 2:24. Judah's gaon, pride, is what God says He will ruin like that spoiled garment. And the piercing question about the leopard's chabarburah, spots, exposes that Judah's evil has become as fixed as an animal's markings, requiring not mere willpower but a new heart.
basic.typology: The loincloth meant to cling closely to Jeremiah pictures the intimate covenant bond God intended with His people, the same clinging language used of marriage in Genesis 2:24, later applied to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. The impossibility of self-reform, a leopard cannot change its spots, anticipates the New Testament's insistence that only a new birth, not self-improvement, can change the human heart, John 3:3.
basic.christ: The intimacy God intended, Israel clinging to Him as closely as a garment to the waist, for His renown and praise and glory, finds its fulfillment in the union between Christ and His church, described in the same terms of one flesh closeness, Ephesians 5:31-32. Where Jeremiah exposes that habitual sin cannot be undone by willpower alone, the gospel answers with what the law could not do, God sending His own Son to give a new heart and new birth, Romans 8:3, John 3:3.
basic.god: God intended nothing less than the closest possible intimacy with His people, clinging as a loincloth clings to the waist, all for His own renown, praise, and glory. His judgment on pride is real and severe, yet even His most piercing rhetorical question, can the leopard change its spots, is not spoken to crush hope but to expose the depth of a problem only He can solve.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2:24 uses the same verb, cling, for the closeness of marriage that God intended with His people. Ephesians 5:31-32 applies this one flesh closeness to Christ and the church. John 3:3 insists that only a new birth, not self-effort, can change a person. Romans 8:3 explains that God did what the law, and human willpower, could never do.
basic.oneStory: This is the exposure that sin runs deeper than willpower can reach, pictured in a ruined garment and an unchangeable leopard, yet it sits within a story that always intended the closest possible intimacy between God and His people, an intimacy sin could ruin but could not, in the end, defeat, since Christ secures the new birth and new heart no self-effort could ever produce.

context.literary:
Chapter 13 is built like a stage play in four scenes, and each scene hangs on a piece of clothing or drink. The first, verses 1 to 11, is written in first person prose and is an obedience narrative: the LORD speaks, Jeremiah does exactly what he is told, and the result is then explained. The phrases 'as the LORD had instructed me' in verse 2 and 'as the LORD commanded me' in verse 5 are the narrator's way of telling us that the prophet is a man under orders. The word of the LORD comes 'a second time,' verse 3, and then again after the cloth is ruined, verse 8, so that the story has three speeches framing two journeys.

The second scene, verses 12 to 14, is a riddle spoken as a toast. The saying 'Every wineskin shall be filled with wine' is an ordinary proverb the audience will have heard at a feast, and when they answer that of course they know it, the saying is turned into a threat. The third scene, verses 15 to 19, is poetry and pleading, with a direct address to the king and the queen mother. The fourth, verses 20 to 27, turns to Jerusalem as a woman in disgrace and ends on the question 'How long will you remain unclean?'

A thread of clothing runs through the whole. A man's waist covering is spoiled in the opening scene, kings lose their crowns in the third, and in the last Jerusalem's skirts are pulled up and her body exposed, verses 22 and 26. The garment that was meant to adorn and cling is first ruined, then stripped.

Pride is the other thread, and the passage varies its vocabulary for it. Three words from the family of height and swelling appear, one in verse 9 for the 'pride of Judah,' one in verse 15 in the command 'Do not be arrogant,' and one in verse 17 in 'because of your pride.' Each of the first three scenes has its version of the sin. And 'listen' recurs: they would not listen, verses 10 and 11, listen and give heed, verse 15, and if you do not listen, verse 17. The chapter is a case study of the hearing that chapter 11 required.
context.historical:
The sign act depends on a fact of ancient dress. A loincloth was worn against the body, below the outer garment, and a linen one was a priest's garment, since the law required linen undergarments for the priests who served at the altar, Exodus 28:42. Jeremiah was a priest, Jeremiah 1:1, so this is an item that he would naturally have worn. It was personal, close and clean, and it was this item that was to lie in the ground until it was ruined. The instruction not to let it touch water means he was not to wash it; its condition when he dug it up could therefore only be the result of what happened in the ground.

Where was Perath? The Hebrew word is the usual name for the Euphrates, and the BSB footnote says it may be the river, in which case Jeremiah made two journeys of hundreds of miles to the edge of Babylon's land and back. But there was also a place called Parah in Benjamin, Joshua 18:23, close to Anathoth, and a spring in the wadi near there has often been proposed. The sign works either way. If it is the Euphrates, the cloth rots in the country of the empire that will take Judah captive. If it is the nearby Parah, the humiliation happens at home. The story is not told to settle geography.

The king and the queen mother of verse 18 are most naturally Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta, who reigned for three months and were taken to Babylon in 597 BC, 2 Kings 24:8-15, as Jeremiah later announces, 22:24-26, and as 29:2 recalls. The queen mother, in Judah, held an office of real power, as the removal of Maacah from that position by Asa shows, 1 Kings 15:13. If this reading is right, the chapter dates to the weeks just before the first deportation, when the closing of the Negev cities, verse 19, and the report from the north, verse 20, were already pressing. A date under Jehoiakim cannot be excluded, since the text names neither king.

The proverb about the Cushite concerns someone from the upper Nile region, as the BSB footnote says. Judah knew Cush as a distant, well known land, and it had known Cushite soldiers and rulers in the days of Hezekiah. A Cushite also appears later in Jeremiah as a man who saves the prophet's life, 38:7-13, which is a useful reminder that the saying uses skin colour only as a picture of something fixed.
context.canonical:
The sign act belongs to a family. Isaiah walked about stripped of his outer garment as a sign against Egypt and Cush, Isaiah 20:2, and was told to write a name on a scroll, Isaiah 8:1. Hosea was told to marry a woman of unfaithful habits, Hosea 1:2, and Ezekiel shaved his head and divided the hair, Ezekiel 5:1. Jeremiah himself later shatters a clay jar, 19:1-10, wears a yoke, 27:2, and buys a field, 32:6-9. In the New Testament the prophet Agabus takes Paul's belt and binds his own hands and feet with it, Acts 21:11, which shows that the form was still alive, and Jesus' own actions in the temple and at the foot washing, John 13:4-5, have something of the same quality, being deeds that carry a message.

The words of verse 11 reach back to Deuteronomy. 'For My renown and praise and glory' gathers three words that the law had spoken of Israel's future, that God would set them 'high in praise and name and honor above all the nations He has made,' Deuteronomy 26:19. The verb 'cling' goes back to Genesis 2:24 and to the way Deuteronomy tells Israel to 'hold fast' to God, Deuteronomy 10:20 and 30:20, where God Himself is called 'your life.' Jeremiah is saying that the privileges of Deuteronomy have been lost because the clinging was lost.

The cup of verse 13 belongs to the cup of wrath that Jeremiah is told to give the nations to drink, 25:15-29, and to Isaiah 51:17, where Jerusalem is told she has drunk it to the dregs. It is also the cup in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:39, and the wine of God's wrath in Revelation 14:10.

The leopard proverb has its New Testament companions in Paul's cry about the law that he cannot carry out, Romans 7:18, 24-25, and in Jesus' saying about the new birth, John 3:3-5. The answer to the problem is that of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26-27: God will put His law within them and give them a new heart.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah wants his hearers to see a thing happen so that they cannot forget it. A message told in words can be argued with, but a rotting loincloth cannot. He is also deliberately intimate: the belt was his own, worn next to his body. The sign makes the point that the relationship between the LORD and His people was meant to be close and personal, not a distant arrangement. The people had been made to cling, and clinging had a purpose, namely that the world might see God's renown through them.

He wants them to understand that pride is the thing that spoils. The obvious sins of Judah, idolatry and injustice, grow from a root of self-importance that the passage names first, 'the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem,' verse 9. The call to 'give glory to the LORD your God before He brings darkness,' verse 16, shows what pride refuses: to hand the weight of glory back to the One to whom it belongs.

He also means to move them to grief. The weeping of verse 17, whoever is weeping, is a sign that the message of judgment is not delivered with satisfaction. And the closing question is not a taunt but a diagnosis. Jeremiah wants his hearers to see that they cannot repair themselves, so that they will cry to the One who can. A sermon that left them merely ashamed would have failed; it was meant to point them to the God who alone can change them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a prophet's assignment and the nation's condition. It does not tell believers to bury clothing or to stage sign acts, and it does not give grounds for thinking that any people is naturally and permanently incapable of change. The proverb of the Cushite and the leopard uses skin and spots as an image of a habit so fixed that willpower cannot unpick it. It says nothing about any ethnic group, and the Bible's own record of Cushites, the man who rescued Jeremiah, Jeremiah 38:7-13, and the official who believed in Acts 8:27-39, should keep readers from ever turning the image into an argument about race.

What does carry forward is a description of ourselves. Ingrained habits do not yield to resolution alone, and people who are 'accustomed to doing evil' need something done to them and not only by them. The hope does not lie in giving up on change but in knowing where it comes from. The same book says, 'I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33. The prescriptive part is therefore the humility to ask for it, and the call of verse 16 to give glory to God now, while there is still light, rather than waiting until darkness has fallen.

debates.question: Did Jeremiah really travel to the Euphrates, or is the story told some other way?

views.label: A literal journey to the Euphrates
views.case: The Hebrew name Perath normally refers to the Euphrates, and the BSB footnote says 'possibly to the Euphrates; similarly in verses 5 to 7.' Two long trips would make the sign costly and memorable, and the Euphrates places the rotting cloth where Judah's captors live. Prophets did sometimes undertake demanding acts, as Ezekiel 4 shows.

views.label: A literal trip to a nearby spring
views.case: A place named Parah is listed in Benjamin, Joshua 18:23, near Anathoth, and a wadi with a spring there has been proposed. The journey would then be easy and could be repeated unnoticed. The two names are similar enough that a copyist or reader could have taken one for the other.

views.label: A vision or a told parable
views.case: Some read the account as a vision or as a parable rehearsed in words, since the long travel is hard to imagine. They note that Jeremiah's other sign acts, like the potter in 18:1-6 and the baskets of figs in 24:1-3, are plainly meant as lessons whether or not every detail is literal.

debates.bearing: The meaning is secure on all three readings. The cloth that was meant to cling to the waist is ruined by what happened to it away from its owner, which is what pride and other gods do to a people who were meant to cling to God.

debates.question: Who is weeping in verse 17?

views.label: The LORD
views.case: The sentence is written in the language of God's own speech, 'I will weep in secret,' in the middle of an oracle. Jeremiah 9:1 and 14:17 give similar tears, and Jesus weeps over Jerusalem in Luke 19:41-44 and Matthew 23:37. A God who weeps because His flock is taken captive fits what chapter 12 has just shown of His grief.

views.label: Jeremiah
views.case: The prophet is the one who weeps elsewhere, and in the Hebrew the weeping is 'my soul' and 'my eyes,' words that suit a human speaker. 'The LORD's flock' is then spoken of in the third person, as in 'the LORD has spoken' in verse 15. The tears are the prophet's response to his message.

views.label: Both
views.case: In prophetic speech the lines between the messenger and the sender are thin, and a prophet who shares God's heart speaks God's tears as his own. The ambiguity may be intentional.

debates.bearing: The tears on either reading are those of someone who loves the flock. The passage will not allow us to hear the warning as delivered with relish, and Jesus takes up the same tears at the sight of Jerusalem.

debates.question: Does the leopard question say that real change is impossible?

views.label: Impossible by one's own power
views.case: The question is rhetorical and has the answer 'no.' It describes people 'accustomed to doing evil,' and the Hebrew behind 'accustomed' comes from the root for being taught or trained, so the picture is of long habit. Jeremiah 17:9 calls the heart deceitful above all things and beyond cure.

views.label: Impossible apart from God, possible with Him
views.case: The same book promises a new covenant with the law inscribed on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and Ezekiel promises a new heart, Ezekiel 36:26. Jesus says that what is impossible with man is possible with God, Matthew 19:26. On this reading the question presses the hearers toward the God who does what they cannot.

views.label: A statement about the particular generation
views.case: Some read the question as a verdict on Judah at this moment, a nation so far gone that only judgment will reach it. Chapter 13 itself never promises a quick change, and the later promise of restoration comes after exile.

debates.bearing: These views do not compete for long. The question rules out self-repair, and the book later answers it with a gift.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb of verse 11, davaq, 'cling,' is the word Genesis 2:24 uses where the BSB has a man 'united' to his wife. Elsewhere Ruth 1:14 uses it of Ruth, who 'clung' to Naomi, and Deuteronomy 10:20 and 30:20 command Israel to 'hold fast' to the LORD, adding that He is their life. So the sign belongs to the vocabulary of marriage and loyalty, not merely of dress. The point of the clinging is given in the three nouns that follow, 'renown and praise and glory.' The same three words appear in Deuteronomy 26:19 in a different order, as the destiny God has set for Israel. When Jeremiah reaches verses 18 and 20, the BSB's 'glorious crowns' and 'the sheep that were your pride' use the same word for glory again. The glory that was to attach to God through His people has fallen from the king's head and has gone from the flock.

Pride appears under three forms. In verse 9 the word is the one used for the swelling of Judah's grandeur, and Leviticus 26:19 uses it of the 'stubborn pride' God will break. In verse 15 the command 'Do not be arrogant' comes from a verb of being high, and in verse 17 'your pride' is another noun from the same family. The people have lifted themselves up, and the sign says what happens to what is lifted up and kept from its owner.

The word translated 'wineskin' in verse 12, nevel, can also mean a clay jar, as in Lamentations 4:2 and Isaiah 30:14. That helps explain the threat of verse 14, which says the people will be smashed against one another, a verb that suits pottery and not leather. A toast that sounds like a blessing becomes a promise of breaking.

In verse 16 'glory' is kavod, whose root has the sense of weight. To give glory is to acknowledge God's weight, and the opposite is the lightness of those who live as if He has none. Joshua uses the same phrase with Achan, 'give glory to the LORD,' and the context there is confession, Joshua 7:19. The 'dusky mountains' of that verse are mountains at twilight, where a foot can stumble because the light is failing, and the next clause says that the light they hope for will be turned to deep gloom.

The shaming in verse 22, according to the footnote, is literally 'your heels have suffered violence,' a way of speaking of mistreatment that leaves a person exposed. The 'lustful neighings' of verse 27 are the sound of stallions, and the same picture appears in Jeremiah 5:8, 'each neighing after his neighbor's wife.'

In verse 23 the question is built on the word for a Cushite, as the footnote records, someone from the upper Nile, and on the word for 'accustomed,' which comes from the root for being taught. The verse literally speaks of those 'taught' to do evil. Habit has become a pupil's second nature. And in verse 25 the nation has 'trusted in falsehood,' sheqer, the same word that chapter 10 used of the molten images as a fraud, 10:14. The person who trusts a lie becomes a living image of it.

typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 11:5 says that the Messiah will have righteousness as the belt around His hips and faithfulness as the sash around His waist. Where Judah's belt is ruined, His does not rot. Believers are said to be united to Him in a bond like marriage, Ephesians 5:31-32, and to be one spirit with Him, 1 Corinthians 6:17, and they 'clothe' themselves with Christ, Galatians 3:27 and Romans 13:14. The correspondence is closeness for the sake of glory. The type falls short because Judah's belt was an object, while Christ is a person who holds His people fast.

typology.type: The cloth that rots in the ground, Jeremiah 13:7
typology.fulfillment: The loincloth decays when it is buried. Peter and Paul stress that Christ's body did not, quoting David, 'nor did His body see decay,' Acts 2:31, and Acts 13:34-37. The contrast is the type: a ruined garment hidden in the ground is answered by a body laid in a tomb that does not decay but rises. The relationship is not predictive but contrastive, because Jeremiah is not speaking of the resurrection, but the New Testament uses the contrast of corruption and incorruption in just these terms.

Every wineskin will be filled, and the leaders and people will be made drunk with judgment. Isaiah 51:17 speaks of the cup of His fury, and Revelation 14:10 of the cup of His wrath. In Gethsemane Jesus prays, 'let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The escalation is that the Son takes the cup that was prepared for others. The type falls short in that Judah drank for her own sin, while He drank for the sin of others, so that those who trust Him are not left to drain it.

typology.type: Give glory before the darkness, Jeremiah 13:16
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah warns that the light they wait for will be turned to deep gloom. Jesus says 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and urges, 'Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you,' John 12:35. When He weeps over Jerusalem He says that she did not recognise the time of her visitation, Luke 19:41-44. The correspondence is real: the offer of light has a limit. The type falls short because Jeremiah only announces the darkness, whereas Christ Himself enters it for the sake of those who would stumble.

Jeremiah's question has its answer in a promise: God will give a new heart and put His Spirit within, Ezekiel 36:26-27. Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom without being born again, John 3:3, and Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17. The escalation is from the despair of the question to the gift. The correspondence is partial: it is a theme and not a strict type, because Jeremiah offers no promise in the chapter itself and leaves that to chapter 31.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the picture of the belt. The Messiah promised in Isaiah 11:5 has 'righteousness' as the belt around His hips and 'faithfulness' as the sash around His waist. Jeremiah's belt is spoiled and useless, the people who were meant to cling to God were spoiled and useless, and then Isaiah describes a King whose belt cannot be spoiled because it is righteousness itself. When Jesus wraps a towel around His waist and washes the disciples' feet, John 13:4-5, He takes the servant's belt, and John tells us He did it knowing that He had come from God and was going to God. In Revelation 1:13 the risen Lord is seen with a golden sash around His chest. The belt that Judah ruined is worn without a stain by the One who keeps the covenant.

It leads to Christ through the union the sign pictures. God wanted a people who clung to Him as a garment clings, and the New Testament says that this union is fulfilled in Christ and the church. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, the very passage whose verb is used in Jeremiah 13:11, and says 'I am speaking about Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:31-32. Whoever is united to the Lord is one spirit with Him, 1 Corinthians 6:17, and Jesus says 'Remain in Me, and I will remain in you,' John 15:4. Believers are said to have clothed themselves with Christ, Galatians 3:27. The thing that Judah's pride destroyed, a people who bear God's renown, is rebuilt in Him, and the church is given 'fine linen, bright and pure,' which Revelation 19:8 says is the righteous acts of the saints.

It leads to Christ by contrast with decay. The loincloth rotted in the earth. Peter says that David foresaw the resurrection of the Christ, 'that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay,' Acts 2:31. Where Judah's garment was ruined by being hidden from its wearer, Christ's body, laid in a rock tomb, was not ruined, and the first Easter is the counterpart to the rotted cloth.

It leads to Christ by the cup. The drunkenness of verses 12 to 14 is the cup of God's anger. Jesus prays in Gethsemane, 'let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and He drinks it so that His people do not have to.

It leads to Christ by the weeping and the light. The tears of verse 17 are taken up when Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41-44, and when He says 'how often I have longed to gather your children together ... but you were unwilling,' Matthew 23:37. Jeremiah's call to give glory before the darkness falls matches Jesus' call to walk while there is light, John 12:35. In both cases the offer is real and has a limit.

Most of all it leads to Christ by the question about the leopard. The question exposes what Romans 7:18 confesses: 'the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out.' It is answered in the next verse by 'What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord,' Romans 7:24-25, and by 'what the law was powerless to do ... God did by sending His own Son,' Romans 8:3. The new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26 and the law written within in Jeremiah 31:33 are given in the new birth, John 3:3-5 and Titus 3:5. When Jesus says that with man this is impossible but with God all things are possible, Matthew 19:26, He speaks to the same kind of impossibility as the leopard's spots.

A caution is needed. The belt is not a code for Jesus, and the details of the sign act do not supply a hidden gospel. The links are those that the New Testament draws: Isaiah's belt, the union of Christ and the church, the incorruptible body, the cup, and the new birth. The chapter supplies the problem, a people who cannot clean themselves, and Christ supplies what it lacks.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is the purpose of His choosing. He made His people cling to Him 'so that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory,' verse 11. This is not the language of a God who needs worshippers to fill a gap; it says that His glory is the end for which Israel exists and that the way He gets it is through closeness. The relationship is for something, and the purpose is that the nations may see what a people near to Him look like. A God who creates a people in order to be glorified through them is not self-absorbed, since His glory is also their good, as Deuteronomy 10:20 and 30:20 say when it calls Him their life.

He is a God of patient instruction. The sign act is drawn out, with two journeys, a long wait, and three speeches, and the teaching rests on a slow demonstration. He could have simply announced the verdict. Instead He asks His prophet to carry a garment to a distant place and to see it spoil, so that no one can mistake what He means. The God who 'sends again and again,' as chapter 11 has said, teaches again and again.

He is a God who judges pride. The word is used three times in this chapter in different forms, and the sentence that falls on it is humiliating: the king and queen mother take a lowly seat, the flock is taken away, and the proud city is stripped. Pride is resisted because it takes from God the weight that belongs to Him. Yet He does not say 'be humble' only as a rule. He offers a way to avoid the darkness: 'Give glory to the LORD your God before He brings darkness.' Judgment is announced in order that it may be avoided.

He is also moved. Verse 17 says that if they will not listen, someone will 'weep in secret.' Whether the speaker is the prophet or the LORD, the weeping belongs to the God who commissioned the prophet to deliver the message. The verse is a rebuke to any picture of a God who takes pleasure in destroying. The same chapter that says 'I will smash them against one another' and 'allow no mercy or pity or compassion to keep Me from destroying them,' verse 14, also says that He weeps. We should keep these together. The verdict is fixed for those who persist, but the heart behind it is wounded, and the chapter will not let either half stand alone.

He is holy and clean. The final question, 'How long will you remain unclean?', assumes that God cares about purity and that His people's state matters to Him. It also assumes that the answer will lie with Him. Only He can cleanse, and the sorrow in the question is the sorrow of a God who longs to do it.

For worship the passage gives us two things to say. First, give glory now, in the light, since the time to do so is while we can still see. Second, confess that we cannot change ourselves, and ask the God who made us cling to Him to keep us there.

crossReferences.note: A man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh. The verb for 'united' is the same as the verb for 'cling' in Jeremiah 13:11. The text from the beginning of Scripture is thus brought to the sign act, making the loincloth a picture of marriage-like closeness between God and His people.

God promises to set Israel high in praise, name and honor above all the nations. The three words correspond to Jeremiah's 'renown and praise and glory' in 13:11. It shows that what God meant the clinging to produce was Israel's destiny as a people who display His name, which Judah's pride has now lost.

Israel is commanded to fear the LORD, serve Him, hold fast to Him, and swear by His name. The verb 'hold fast' is the same as 'cling' in Jeremiah 13:11. Moses ties clinging to worship and to oaths, which shows that the loincloth is a picture of obedient loyalty and not only of feeling.

Righteousness will be the belt around the Messiah's hips and faithfulness the sash around His waist. The belt, the very item that Jeremiah's people ruined, becomes in Isaiah the clothing of the coming King. It sets the failure of Judah beside the faithfulness of Christ.

Jeremiah is told to take the cup of the wine of wrath and make the nations drink so that they stagger and go out of their minds. It is the larger picture of which the filled wineskins of 13:12-14 are a part. The drunkenness of judgment falls on kings, priests, and prophets here, and on all nations there.

God says that even if Coniah were a signet ring on His right hand, He would pull him off and hurl him and his mother into another land. It gives the history behind 13:18, where the king and queen mother lose their crowns, and it shows how seriously the prophet took the deportation of Jehoiachin.

Ebed-melech the Cushite, a court official, hears that Jeremiah has been put into a cistern and pleads with the king to save him. It shows a Cushite acting rightly where Judah's own leaders did not, which cautions against reading 13:23 as a statement about any people.

God promises to put His law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts, and to forgive their iniquities. It is the book's own reply to the leopard question of 13:23, for it promises the change that Judah cannot produce for itself.

God will give a new heart and put His Spirit within them so that they walk in His statutes. It states the promise behind the rhetorical question of Jeremiah 13:23 and names the means: not the people's effort but the Spirit's work.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem because she did not know the things that make for peace and did not recognise the time of her visitation. It fulfils in the person of Christ the weeping of Jeremiah 13:17 and the warning of darkness before it falls.

Jesus says that the Light will be among them a little longer and tells them to walk while they have the Light so that darkness will not overtake them. The warning of Jeremiah 13:16 to give glory before darkness comes is given again, with the Light now identified as Christ.

Paul confesses that nothing good lives in his flesh and that he cannot carry out the good he desires, and then asks who will rescue him from this body of death. The cry is the New Testament's version of Jeremiah 13:23, and its answer, 'Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord,' is the gospel's reply.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 2:24 introduces the verb of this chapter, and Genesis 3 shows its loss. The man and woman who were united in Eden, and who walked with God in the cool of the day, hid when they heard Him and covered themselves with leaves, Genesis 3:7-8. Jeremiah's loincloth is a garment ruined, and the stripping of Jerusalem's skirts in verses 22 and 26 is the shame of Eden exposed again. Pride was already there at the beginning, in the desire to be like God, Genesis 3:5. What Judah displays is old.

The story of Israel runs along the same line. God chose a people to be His treasured possession and a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:5-6, and set them high in praise, name and honour, Deuteronomy 26:19. The prophets then chronicle the failure. Hosea's marriage, Isaiah's vineyard, and Jeremiah's belt are the same story told with different objects: the people God joined to Himself have turned from Him. The punishment is also the same. The garden's exile becomes the exile to Babylon, and the king, the queen mother and the flock are carried out of the land in the shape of Genesis 3:23-24.

But chapter 13 also sets up what comes next. By asking the question of the leopard it shows that the problem is deeper than behaviour. God Himself must give a new heart. The book that records this question answers it in chapter 31 by promising a covenant in which the law is written within, and Ezekiel names the means as a new heart and the Spirit. When Jesus says that no one can see the kingdom without being born again, John 3:3, He is speaking to a teacher of Israel who should have known these promises.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who is the Messiah girded with righteousness, who drinks the cup, who weeps over Jerusalem and then dies outside her walls, whose body does not decay, and who unites His people to Himself so that they are clothed in Him, Galatians 3:27. The Cushite who cannot change his skin finds a counterpart in Acts, where a Cushite official of Candace's court reads Isaiah on the road and is baptised, Acts 8:26-39. The person Jeremiah used to illustrate the unchangeable is among the first outside Israel to be changed.

At the end of the story the clinging is complete. The church is the bride prepared for the Lamb and dressed in fine linen, bright and pure, Revelation 19:7-8. The darkness that Jeremiah feared has no place in the city, where there is no night and the Lord God gives light, Revelation 22:5, and no one is left unclean, since nothing impure can enter it, Revelation 21:27. The people God made to cling to Him for His renown and praise and glory have become what He intended, and the glory is His.

sermon.title: Christmas at the Castle, Part 3
sermon.why: Carson expounds the linen girdle and the smashed wine jars of Jeremiah 13 as acted parables of Judah's ruined pride, directly the images and message this study walks through.

quiz.q: What happens to the loincloth Jeremiah buries at Perath?

options.text: It is ruined, of no use at all, after being buried many days.
options.note: Verse 7 states this exactly.

options.text: It remains perfectly preserved despite being buried.
options.note: This directly contradicts verse 7, which describes it as ruined.

options.text: It is stolen by a passing traveler.
options.note: Not described anywhere in the passage.

options.text: It becomes more valuable with age, like fine wine.
options.note: The opposite happens; the garment is spoiled, not enhanced.

quiz.q: What does the ruined loincloth represent, according to 13:9-11?

options.text: The pride of Judah and Jerusalem, ruined because Israel refused to cling to the LORD as intended.
options.note: Verses 9-11 explain this meaning directly.

options.text: God's own faithfulness beginning to fail.
options.note: The opposite; the sign pictures Judah's ruin, not any failure in God's faithfulness.

options.text: The wealth of surrounding foreign nations.
options.note: Not the meaning given in the text; the sign concerns Judah specifically.

options.text: The coming destruction of the temple building itself.
options.note: The sign concerns Judah's pride and closeness to God broadly, not the temple building specifically.

quiz.q: What image does God use in 13:12-14 for the coming judgment?

options.text: Every wineskin filled with wine, then everyone, including kings and priests, smashed against one another in drunkenness.
options.note: Verses 12-14 use this exact image.

options.text: A city rebuilt after its earlier destruction.
options.note: This contradicts the judgment imagery of the passage, which pictures ruin, not rebuilding.

options.text: A flock scattered across distant mountains.
options.note: This image appears elsewhere in Jeremiah, but not in this specific unit.

options.text: A field left fallow for seven years.
options.note: Not the image used in this passage; the specific picture is of wineskins and drunkenness.

quiz.q: According to 13:18, who besides the general population is told to take a lowly seat?

options.text: The king and the queen mother, because their glorious crowns have fallen from their heads.
options.note: Verse 18 addresses these specific figures.

options.text: The prophets who opposed Jeremiah's message.
options.note: Not the specific addressees named in verse 18.

options.text: Foreign ambassadors visiting Jerusalem.
options.note: Not mentioned anywhere in this verse.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: Not the specific figures named in verse 18; the king and queen mother are addressed directly.

quiz.q: What does the question about the Ethiopian's skin and the leopard's spots in 13:23 illustrate?

options.text: That Judah's habitual evil has become so ingrained that they cannot simply reform themselves by effort alone.
options.note: Verse 23 draws this exact conclusion, neither are you able to do good.

options.text: That people can easily change their behavior through willpower alone.
options.note: This directly contradicts the point of the rhetorical question.

options.text: That only foreign nations are capable of deep, ingrained sin.
options.note: The passage applies this point directly to Judah, not exclusively to foreign nations.

options.text: That God unfairly judges people for features they cannot help.
options.note: This misreads the analogy, which concerns ingrained moral habit, not an unfair judgment based on physical features.

questions: The loincloth was meant to cling closely to Jeremiah, just as Israel was meant to cling to the LORD. What competes for the place of closeness God intends to have with you?
Judah's pride is pictured as a ruined, useless garment. Where might pride be quietly ruining something valuable in your own life or relationships?
Even the king and queen mother were told to take a lowly seat before God. What position of pride or status might you need to lay down before Him?

The question, can a leopard change its spots, exposes that some patterns of sin run deeper than willpower can fix. Where have you been trying to change something in your own strength that actually needs God's transforming work?
God intended Israel's closeness to Him to be for His own renown, praise, and glory. How does knowing that your closeness to God brings Him praise change how you approach Him today?

translationNotes.note: Perath most likely refers to the Euphrates river, though some propose a nearer wadi or village of similar name; either reading preserves the symbolic distance and difficulty of the journey involved in the sign act.
The queen mother held a position of real political influence in Judah's royal court, so her humbling alongside the king signals total, not merely symbolic, national disgrace.
Ethiopian translates a word referring to the Cushite region south of Egypt; the illustration concerns unchangeable, natural features, not any moral judgment on that people themselves.
